node.title: Mitochondrial DNA mutations and maternal inheritance
node.canonical_question: What mutations in mitochondrial DNA cause maternally inherited diseases?
node.summary: Point mutations and large deletions in mitochondrial DNA can disrupt oxidative phosphorylation subunits or tRNAs, causing diseases like MELAS and MERRF. Because mitochondria are inherited almost entirely from the egg, these diseases pass from mother to all children.

render.title: Mitochondrial DNA mutations and maternal inheritance
render.body:
Mitochondria carry their own small loop of DNA, separate from the chromosomes in the nucleus. This mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) encodes 13 proteins that are part of the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, plus the RNA molecules the mitochondrion needs to build them.

When a mutation arises in mtDNA it can interfere with energy production directly. Two well-known examples:

- MELAS (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes): most commonly caused by an A-to-G point mutation at position 3243 in the gene for a transfer RNA. This faulty tRNA disrupts the synthesis of several respiratory chain subunits, reducing ATP output and raising lactic acid levels.

- MERRF (Myoclonic Epilepsy with Ragged-Red Fibres): usually caused by a point mutation at position 8344, also in a tRNA gene, leading to muscle weakness and seizures.

Large deletions of mtDNA (removing hundreds or thousands of base pairs) cause conditions such as Kearns-Sayre syndrome and Pearson syndrome by wiping out multiple subunit genes at once.

Why maternal inheritance? When a sperm fertilises an egg, the sperm contributes almost no mitochondria — the cytoplasm of the egg supplies essentially all of them. So every child inherits their mitochondrial DNA from their mother. A mother who carries a pathogenic mtDNA mutation can pass it to all her children, but an affected father does not pass it on.

One complicating factor is heteroplasmy: a cell can contain a mixture of normal and mutant mtDNA copies. Symptoms tend to appear only when the proportion of mutant copies exceeds a tissue-specific threshold, which is why severity varies even within the same family.

This connects back to energy production: when enough respiratory chain proteins are non-functional, cells in high-energy-demand tissues — brain, muscle, heart — cannot produce sufficient ATP, which explains the neurological and muscular symptoms typical of mitochondrial diseases.
